input.question: Which educational institution did Philip Lowrie attend?

documents.text: As the sun set over the bustling streets of Fukuoka, Philip Lowrie strolled through the campus of Kyushu University, his worn leather satchel slung over his shoulder. It was a crisp autumn evening in 1965, and the British actor, fresh from his breakout role in the BBC's "Coronation Street," had just arrived in Japan to immerse himself in the language and culture. Philip had always been drawn to the exotic and the unknown, and his fascination with Japan had begun years earlier, when he stumbled upon a dog-eared copy of "The Tale of Genji" in a used bookstore in Manchester. The intricate woodblock prints and whispers of samurai honor had captivated him, and he knew that he had to experience it all firsthand. As he walked through the university's gates, Philip was struck by the vibrant colors of the koyo, the changing leaves of the maple trees that seemed to glow in the fading light. He felt a sense of excitement and trepidation, knowing that he was about to embark on a journey that would challenge him in ways he never thought possible. Professor Tanaka, a kind-eyed linguist with a passion for Shakespeare, greeted Philip warmly and led him to the small apartment that would be his home for the next few months. Over steaming cups of green tea, they discussed Philip's goals and expectations, and the professor presented him with a stack of textbooks and a schedule that would keep him busy from dawn till dusk. As the days turned into weeks, Philip threw himself into his studies, determined to master the complexities of the Japanese language. He practiced his kanji with a group of giggling students, who teased him good-naturedly about his accent and his tendency to confuse left and right. He devoured bowls of steaming ramen at the campus cafeteria, marveling at the flavors and textures that danced on his tongue. And yet, despite the demands of his coursework, Philip found himself drawn to the university's theater troupe, a group of passionate students who were staging a production of "Hamlet" in Japanese. He watched from the shadows, mesmerized by their energy and dedication, and soon found himself offering to help with the set design and coaching the actors on their delivery. As the weeks turned into months, Philip's fluency in Japanese grew, and with it, his appreciation for the nuances of the culture.
